title: Atletico Madrid 1 Arsenal 1 — Why was Eze ‘penalty’ overturned? Were other decisions controversial?
author: Dan Sheldon
content:
It wasn’t the nine goals we were treated to on Tuesday, but this week’s second Champions League semi-final was not short of drama, with two penalties given and one controversially overturned.

Atletico Madrid’s spot kick was similar to the one Paris Saint-Germain received against Bayern Munich on Tuesday, with the ball striking Ben White’s hand. Arsenal’s came when David Hancko bundled over Viktor Gyokeres.

But the most controversial was the third, originally awarded after Eberechi Eze was caught by Hancko, but then overturned when the referee went to the VAR screen. Just down the touchline, Atletico manager Diego Simeone was making his feelings known.

It was an intimidating atmosphere in the Metropolitano from the start, as the teams were welcomed by toilet roll streaming down from the stands. Before a ball was kicked, Arsenal lodged a complaint with UEFA over the pitch’s condition, an issue raised by previous opponents.

As it was, Mikel Arteta’s side will feel they should have come away with a lead, especially after the overturned penalty call.

The second leg will be played at the Emirates on Tuesday, with the winner facing either Bayern Munich or PSG in the final.

James McNicholas, Dan Sheldon, Dermot Corrigan, Anantaajith Raghuraman, Jack Lang and former Premier League referee Graham Scott help break down the action.

Arsenal had the perfect first half, weathering an early Atletico storm and enduring a hostile atmosphere to steadily gain control of the game. Gyokeres’ emphatic penalty shortly before half-time put Arteta’s team in a commanding position.

The second half was a different story. This Atletico team rely heavily on momentum, and after the break, they built a series of successive attacks. Arteta made changes, introducing Eze and changing his entire front line, but Arsenal could not regain control.

Arsenal may have lost control on the night, but they regained their composure in those final stages. What’s more, with home advantage in the second leg, they arguably still have control of the tie.

James McNicholas

The third big penalty call of the night turned out to be arguably the most controversial.

When referee Danny Makkelie pointed to the spot after Eze went to ground, the complaints from Atletico players and supporters seemed relatively muted.

But the noise rose through the VAR check, and Simeone was clearly calling from the sideline for Makkelie to go and have a look at the monitor. The Argentine coach then applauded when he did, and stood as close as he could while the official reviewed the incident on the screen.

Replays suggested that Eze certainly made the most of what contact there was — and the question seemed to be whether Hancko had made enough to send him flying, or if the midfielder had exaggerated what a light brush.

In the end, Makkelie crossed his arms to gesture that he was changing his mind. There were huge cheers from the Atletico crowd, with Simeone dancing in delight as the two teams got ready to restart play.

Dermot Corrigan

The first half of the match provided little in common from the previous night’s thriller between PSG and Bayern. But a semblance of deja vu arrived 10 minutes into the second half.

After clearing out the toilet paper that Atletico fans threw onto the pitch during the game, Antoine Griezmann lofted a corner to the edge of the box. Marcos Llorente ran onto it and mishit his volley, but it bounced and struck White, with Atletico players instantly putting their hands up and surrounding Makkelie. Simeone was animated on the sidelines, too.

Makkelie initially suggested he did not see the incident but a VAR check was quickly underway and he was asked to look at the screen. The ball could be seen slightly deflecting off White’s knee and hitting his arm as he withdrew it towards his body (below).

Those who caught the action in Paris would have instantly been reminded of the situation involving Alphonso Davies moments before half-time. The Bayern left-back was also moving his hand towards his body when a cross came in from Ousmane Dembele.

UEFA rules were followed consistently, with a penalty awarded for both situations. Handling the ball after it strikes a body part is usually waved away as an accidental handball in the Premier League.

Anantaajith Raghuraman

After the talk of his future pre-game, including Simeone saying he was not surprised that Arsenal were interested in signing him this summer as he was “very good”, there was a lot of focus on Alvarez tonight.

The Argentinian was at the heart of most of Atletico’s best attacking moves in the early stages, roving around the pitch, and arriving late in the area when it suited. He had the first shot on target from either side — a 20-yard curler that Raya pushed around the post.

There was also a half-chance with a header from closer in that flew too high. But then disaster struck when his misdirected header in his own half went straight to Martin Zubimendi, leading directly to the penalty won and converted by Gyokeres.

After the break, Alvarez’s frustrating night continued with a free kick that many in the stadium thought he had scored, before they realised it had hit the side netting. But the game was turning Atletico’s way, and he set up Ademola Lookman for a clear chance that led to the corner from which Simeone’s side were awarded their own spot kick.

Alvarez has endured mixed luck from the spot with Atletico — including last season’s disallowed double-touch penalty as they were eliminated in the last 16 by Real Madrid. But he nervelessly slammed the ball into the net for his 10th Champions League goal of 2025-26 — making him the first Atletico player to reach double figures in one campaign.

For Alvarez, it was a rollercoaster evening, but he will feel he can be even more decisive in next week’s second leg in London.

Dermot Corrigan

Tuesday night was a festival of colour and light, a thousand playground dreams made flesh at the Parc des Princes. Everything PSG and Bayern touched turned to goals. It was a game that lifted the spirits, took the breath away, took the eyeballs for a joy ride.

This was different. The teams spent the first half figuring each other out, shadow boxing. Then, just as it became tempting to moan about the lack of spectacle, the match lurched into something more interesting. The second half was attritional, gritty, intense. There were mistakes. There were cynical fouls. There were jangling nerves and streams of toilet paper on the pitch.

This will not go down in the history books. It was, though, a reminder that this kind of game can be every bit — OK, fine, nearly — as enjoyable as what preceded it.

The penalty awarded to Arsenal just before half-time appeared soft and you can see why Atletico Madrid were incensed.

At the same time, Arsenal would rightly have felt aggrieved if it wasn’t given. After a great one-two exchange between Odegaard and Zubimendi, Gyokres received the ball from Zubimendi inside the area and took a touch.

But just as he did that, Hancko — with both hands wrapped around the forward and the wrong side of him — clattered into the Arsenal striker from behind, with Gyokeres not needing a second invitation to hit the deck.

Soft? Yes. Clumsy on Hancko’s part? Absolutely.

As for whether it could have been a red card for Hancko, former Premier League referee Graham Scott says: “It’s part of a challenge for the ball, so it should not have been a red. Yellow would be justified as Gyokeres’ next action is a shot at goal with only the ‘keeper to beat. It would have been a red roughly five years ago, but there was a law change to stop this kind of double jeopardy.”

Under intense pressure, and in front of the furious home crowd at the Metropolitano who felt an injustice had just occurred, Gyokeres struck it past Jan Oblak to give Arsenal the lead going into half-time.

And as the players headed down the tunnel, Koke, Atletico’s captain, went over to the referee to complain, while Simeone also shook his hand in the official’s direction.

Dan Sheldon and Graham Scott

Arsenal would have arrived at the Metropolitano expecting a hostile atmosphere and tricky playing conditions.

What they may not have prepared for was the need to lodge a complaint with UEFA, the competition’s organiser, over the condition of Atletico’s pitch.

Arsenal were concerned that the increased length of grass would slow the pace of the match, coupled with the watering of the surface increasing the likelihood of players slipping. And those fears were realised in the opening minute of the tie, after Piero Hincapie slipped at the back.

From there, however, the condition of the pitch didn’t appear to make a significant impact.

Dan Sheldon

Speaking to the media, the Arsenal manager was furious that the decision to award his side a second penalty was overturned. “After talking to the boys and watching the penalty incident, I’m extremely disappointed and annoyed,” Arteta said. “It was against the rules, I don’t understand it and it changes the course of the tie. Very, very upset.

“There is clear contact. If you make that decision, you cannot overturn that decision. When you have to look at it 13 times… at this level, it’s completely unacceptable.”

When asked about Atletico’s penalty, Arteta added, “They have been consistent, so if you’re going to give a penalty for that kind of thing, you have to accept it. I have nothing to say on that, but the one that changes everything is on Eze. That cannot happen at this level.”

He was far more satisfied with his players’ performance, insisting they “did a lot of positive things” to put Arsenal “in an incredible position” for the second leg.

Before then, they will host Fulham in the Premier League on Saturday, and Arteta said, “We will make sure the players eat, sleep, get a lot of love and use every hour of the day to be in the position to win.”

Saturday, May 2: Fulham (Home), Premier League, 5.30pm UK, 12.30pm ET
